guardianfootball.title: Lammens errors cost Manchester United victory in frantic finale at Sporting
guardianfootball.description: “We are a strong team,” Mauricio Pochettino exhorted, then watched Manchester United’s unerring ability to cause drama every time they lace up their boots. Cruising, it seemed, at 2-1 and with 10 minutes left, they unravelled, as Senne Lammens dropped a high ball in front of his goal and a grateful Luis Suárez equalised with a bicycle kick. Cut almost instantly to Sporting’s Kaique Pereira who bundled the ball in for United’s apparent winner only for Szymon Marciniak to be ordered to the screen by the video assistant referee, where the official ruled the goal out for a foul on the goalkeeper by Patrick Dorgu. Continue reading...

Glasner was tempted to move to the City Ground by owner Evangelos Marinakis after winning the FA Cup and Conference League at Crystal Palace. However, Forest have won two of their opening 11 Premier League games and sit outside the relegation zone only on goal difference. Continue reading...

Dayot Upamecano opened the scoring for Bayern but Ayase Ueda levelled for Lille before a horror Aleksandar Pavlovic own goal gifted the hosts victory. Bayern’s unbeaten record in all competitions was ended by a Lille side who kicked off in 35th place in the tournament’s league phase. Continue reading...

The Scotland international scored his second goal for the Potters in the 1-0 win over Birmingham on Saturday and doubled his tally for the season to take Stoke back into the automatic promotion places. At the time, Garnacho was a teenage star flourishing on the grandest of stages, a fixture in the United team and fresh from scoring an outrageous overhead kick at Goodison Park a few days earlier that would later clinch the Premier League’s goal-of-the-season…

The former England international, who five years ago was leading the Three Lions’ charge to a European Championship final, stood expressionless in the dock as the sentence was read out by district judge Kirsty Allman at Basingstoke magistrates court. quietus.title: Huge Wings Trying To Fly: Aleksandra Słyż Interviewed
quietus.description: Ahead of a performance of Ruiny/ Ruins as part of Unsound London, the Polish sound artist speaks to Claire Sawers about the fragility of memory and the use of old tech. Portraits: Thomas Zanon-Larcher I Carry the Strength by Aleksandra Słyż “My surname is pronounced ‘swish’,” explains composer Aleksandra Słyż. Ok, I was way off. “In Polish that means hearing,” she tells me. This is a perfect name for a sound artist who describes herself as ‘primarily concerned with the timbral relationships between acoustic and synthetic sounds and the exploration of microtonal tuning systems’. Słyż is wearing a black polo neck, sat in front of rows of electronic equipment. She’s chatting on Zoom, located…

quietus.description: The unveiling of the video marks 40 years since the release of Your Funeral... The archival video was captured on VHS while Cave and band were touring their 1986 albums Your Funeral... The live lineup at the time featured Cave, Mick Harvey, Blixa Bargeld, Thomas Wydler, Kid Congo Powers and Roland Wolf. In addition to releasing the live footage, Cave and band have released a collection of merchandise to mark the 40th…

quietus.title: Deaf Jams: George Clarke of Deafheaven’s Favourite Songs
quietus.description: Following the release of a scorching new EP, the Deafheaven vocalist takes Dan Franklin through his favourite 13 songs, from a longstanding love of hip hop to Nina Simone's most metal moment Photo by Liam Stewart When I speak to George Clarke, frontman of Deafheaven, he is in the sanctum of his car. Still recovering from a lurgy picked up on the road as main support to Mastodon on their North American tour, with friends Alcest opening, his voice starts to wear out as we make our way through his Baker’s Dozen list. Deafheaven’s music continues to take them to interesting new places, and the music itself still surprises. Not least last month's surprise-released EP At Work In The Fields Of…

quietus.title: Kogumaza – You Found Yourself Where You Found Yourself
quietus.description: Kogumaza You Found Yourself Where You Found Yourself Formed in Nottingham in 2009, the drone and ambient rock trio’s first album since 2019’s Fugues is a gorgeous exploration of mantric repetition that hits the ear like a welcome draft of cool but invigorating air You Found Yourself Where You Found Yourself by Kogumaza Despite sharing a family tree with the likes of Rattle, Hey Colossus, Bob Tilton, Wolves Of Greece, Haress and Grey Hairs, Kogumaza always trod their own path. Bands often don’t love the labels that critics stick them with, but ‘post-rock’ is disliked more than most. At their worst, post-rock bands can seem formulaic and lacking in emotion. Kogumaza adroitly avoid falling…

quietus.title: Wilder Maker – Smoking The Bunny
quietus.description: Wilder Maker Smoking The Bunny Partly improvised and partly crooned, the latest from the Brooklyn quartet matches sonic texture to narrative detail Smoking the Bunny by Wilder Maker The last we heard from the reinvigorated Brooklyn outfit Wilder Maker, on their compelling 2025 LP, These Streets Still Warm Like Beds, the Gabe Birnbaum-led quartet left listeners with an unsettling image: “The sea is stronger than the swimmer”. With that sophisticated turn, Wilder Maker not only reinvented their sound but launched the first chapter in a trilogy of improvisation-based albums following a wayward figure…

It was largely built from a process of improvisation. Commenting on the album, Toral said: "Long Ways is a development forward from the previous two albums, but condensing everything into playing guitar. It’s all about sound, or better, the stillness of presence. The music itself here is less important than the sound of playing. What I’m after is an abstraction, the sound of…

quietus.title: TIDAL to Delete and Ban Fully AI-Generated Music

From 9 December, any wholly AI-generated track will be rejected and removed from the platform, while all songs that have already been uploaded and identified as entirely produced using AI will also be deleted from the streaming service. Announcing the change, TIDAL revealed that 43% of all tracks distributed to the platform have been detected as wholly AI-generated over the last 90 days. These tracks have been labelled as such in order…

aquariumdrunkard.title: Late November :: Autumnal Britfolk Instrumentals (1968-1981)
aquariumdrunkard.description: The shadows are lengthening, the leaves are falling, the air is getting crisp. That’s right, we’re heading into the latter days of autumn. Maybe the best time of year? One of them, anyway. The season demands a soundtrack, and for some reason, the loosely organized britfolk genre is perfect for these days. So here’s an hour’s worth of instrumentals from the late 1960s to the early 1980s, when giants walked the earth. Trad melodies and rhythms abound, but there are plenty of left-turns, mostly thanks to dedicated iconoclasts like John Martyn, Davey Graham and Michael Chapman. Grab a pint of something dark and rich and settle in.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Transmissions :: Beth Orton
aquariumdrunkard.description: This week on the show, we’re presenting the penultimate episode of our 12th season. And we’ve saved a tremendous talk for this second to last installment: our guest is singer/songwriter Beth Orton. In the mid-’90s, she emerged as a purveyor of electronic folk, working with artists like William Orbit, The Chemical Brothers, and Four Tet. Her latest is The Ground Above. Reviewing it for Aquarium Drunkard, Kyle Lemmon described it as “a free-flowing mixture of electronic funk, spirit walking jazz, and ambient folk.”

aquariumdrunkard.title: Miles Davis: Copenhagen Live 1969
aquariumdrunkard.description: Miles Davis’ 1969 live ensemble existed in a parallel timeline alongside his studio work - greasing his audience for a future for which they were wholly unprepared. A new 2LP set, Copenhagen Live 1969 , captures the band at its peak, stress-testing then-unreleased Bitches Brew material, tearing it down and reassembling it into some of the most far-out, formless music of Miles’ career.

aquariumdrunkard.title: The Lagniappe Sessions :: Shane Butler
aquariumdrunkard.description: Shane Butler's first solo record, Heavy Debt , is due next month, and for this Lagniappe Session he's pulled together three songs that have been rattling around for a long time. Fugazi's "I'm So Tired," a song he first encountered as a kid watching skate videos, Shoes' homemade pop and a 1979 Soft Boys' nugget.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Frank Black :: The Aquarium Drunkard Interview
aquariumdrunkard.description: In 2025, Pixies leader Frank Black took to the road to celebrate the 30th anniversary of his 1994 sophomore LP Teenager of the Year with the same cast of players who recorded the original album. A sprawling double album, it's held together with the same kind of ramshackle logic that makes The Beatles' The White Album or The Clash's London Calling work. Recently, Aquarium Drunkard caught up with Black to discuss revisiting the album. Along the way, he revealed details about a Pixies record in the works, UFOs, the paranormal, and explained his vision of a future rock & roll cult where artists like The Feelies are elevated to the status of saints.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Fine :: Jazz Dreams
aquariumdrunkard.description: For all the creativity Copenhagen’s avant-pop scene can offer, a lot of it had started to hang on its own clichés. Who knew it could be recharged by a blasé attitude and a good old dose of harmonic complexity? Fine’s Jazz Dreams is full of the kind of drowsy virtuosity that once again justifies the hype over that scene's prolific output; it's as if you were inhabiting the fantasies of a conservatory student who fell asleep in counterpoint class.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Tía Rosa :: Thirteen Automatic Dreams
aquariumdrunkard.description: Via Mexico City, Thirteen Automatic Dreams is the thrillingly comfy new record by Tía Rosa. Here is some minimalist kosmische with a Latin pop sensibility, a bridge between the noisy regularity of Neu! and the sugared melancholy of balada romántica. It all plays like a lost soundtrack to the Nevada desert of the Nocilla Trilogy , where shoes hang from a lonely poplar, or like Stereolab is being collectively hallucinated from one of those little Durango towns where Jodorowsky liked to film his deranged acid westerns.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Sunday Mourners :: A-Rhythm Absolute
aquariumdrunkard.description: Skirting the edges of canonical post-punk, the debut record by four piece Sunday Mourners is a gripping, youthful art-rock explosion. There are distinct flashes tapping into Chairs Missing -era jagged melodicism here, VU at their most intractable jamming there (the twelve minute "Darling" a prime example). Above all, A-Rhythm Absolute is a downright lively listen, hitting all of the spirited guitar-centric benchmarks to make the listener a reinvigorated believer in the state of such a modern landscape.

mubi.title: A World in Parts
mubi.description: The Journey (Peter Watkins, 1987). At Radio Canada, preparations are underway for Ronald Reagan’s 1985 summit with Canadian prime minister Brian Mulroney. Filmmaker Peter Watkins and his crew have been allowed into meetings where the broadcasters plan their coverage down to the second. Everyone must synchronize their watches: A discrepancy of 40 seconds, one participant warns, could throw off the day’s work. A shot requested at 17:02 might be missed if recorded 30 seconds later. “One thing is certain: there can’t be anything unexpected tonight,” another member of the team declares. Security officials will provide the presidential route, street by street, allowing the text to be prepared…
